worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(({x}^{2}-1){e}^{-{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={({x}^{2}-1)}^{′}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}+({x}^{2}-1){({e}^{-{x}^{2}})}^{′} \\  & =2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}+({x}^{2}-1)(-2x){e}^{-{x}^{2}} \\  & =2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}(1-({x}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2x(2-{x}^{2}){e}^{-{x}^{2}} \\  & =-2x({x}^{2}-2){e}^{-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x({x}^{2}-2){e}^{-{x}^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{-{x}^{2}}\ne 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by ${e}^{-{x}^{2}}$ and solve the resulting equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x({x}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ -2x(x-\sqrt{2})(x+\sqrt{2}) & =0 \\ x & =-\sqrt{2},\,0,\,\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-\sqrt{2},$ $x=0,$ and $x=\sqrt{2}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, in ascending order, the critical points of $f(x)$ are

$$
x=-\sqrt{2},\,x=0,\,\text{and}\,x=\sqrt{2}.
$$
